1.title: Twins, Not Copies

lines.text: My guests today are identical twins, Nora and Nell, who are thirty-two and have, er, chosen very different lives. Nora's a surgeon, Nell's a jazz drummer. Welcome, both of you.
Thanks for having us.
Yeah, thanks. We don't usually agree to interviews, so this is a treat.
Let's start with childhood. Were you close?
Very. We were inseparable until we were about twelve. We even enjoyed wearing the same clothes, which seems mad now.
And then I started resenting being "one of the twins". I couldn't stand being compared all the time. Teachers would say, "Your sister finished her homework, why didn't you?"
So how did you deal with that?
I stopped trying to be like Nora. I took up the drums, mostly to annoy everyone, if I'm honest.
It worked. I remember lying in bed and hearing her practise for hours.
Did you drift apart as teenagers?
For a while, yes. There was a lot of sibling rivalry. We avoided talking to each other for most of one summer.
Our mum kept suggesting going on holiday together, just the two of us. We finally agreed, mostly to make her stop asking.
And that trip changed everything. We spent two weeks in Portugal, and we realised we actually got along brilliantly when nobody was comparing us.
What about now? Do you see eye to eye on most things?
On the important things, yes. On music, absolutely not. Nora listens to the radio news while she's operating. I can't imagine doing that.
It helps me concentrate! And I don't mind admitting I can't keep a beat to save my life.
Do people still mix you up?
All the time. A patient once stopped me in the supermarket and kept thanking me for his new hip.
And she just accepted it!
Well, I didn't want to risk upsetting him. I said, "You're very welcome," and walked off.

1.title: The Family Group Chat

lines.text: You're listening to Talkback. Today's topic: the family group chat. Love it or hate it? Lisa's on line one. Lisa, go ahead.
Hi Darren. Look, my problem is that my family never stops messaging. There are fourteen of us in one chat, and my phone buzzes from six in the morning.
Fourteen! What sort of things do they send?
Everything. Photos of dinner, jokes, er, political videos from my uncle. The thing is, I love them, we're a really close-knit family, but I'm going mad.
Have you thought about leaving the chat?
That's the problem. If I leave, my mum will think something's wrong. The truth is that it's the only way she feels connected to everybody since Dad died.
That's a tricky one. What's the solution, do you think?
My plan is that I mute it during the week and catch up on Sundays. That way nobody gets hurt.
Sounds sensible. Thanks, Lisa. Marco, you're on Talkback.
Hey, Darren. I've got the opposite story, actually. My question is whether a group chat can, um, patch things up.
Go on.
So, my brother and I didn't see eye to eye for years. He was the black sheep, I was the one who stayed near my parents. We drifted apart. Then my niece made a group chat for Grandma's ninetieth.
And that changed things?
Slowly. At first he just sent thumbs-up emojis. But then he started joking with me, and last month we met for a beer. The fact is, I don't think we'd have spoken without that chat.
That's lovely. So the lesson is that it depends how you use it?
Exactly. My view is that the chat isn't good or bad. It's a tool. The danger is when people say things there they'd never say face to face.
Wise words. Thanks, Marco. After the break, we'll hear from a listener whose sister rubs everyone up the wrong way in the chat.

2.title: The Hike That Went Wrong
2.topic: Past obligation, speculation and unsolved mysteries

lines.text: So, are you going to tell me what happened on Saturday, or do I have to read about it in the local paper?
Ha. Don't. Honestly, it wasn't that dramatic. Well, OK, it was a bit dramatic.
You had to be rescued, Maya.
We didn't have to be rescued. A ranger just, er, helped us find the path again. That's different.
Fine. So what went wrong?
Where do I start? First, we should have checked the weather. We didn't, and the fog came down at about two o'clock.
Didn't you have a map?
We had one on Leo's phone. But his battery died. We ought to have brought a paper map. Everyone says that, and we ignored it.
And you were supposed to register at the visitor centre, weren't you? That's the rule on that trail.
We were supposed to, yes. But it was closed when we arrived, so we just went. We shouldn't have done that. Nobody knew where we were.
So how did the ranger find you?
Luckily, my sister knew our plan. When we didn't call by six, she phoned the park. So we didn't have to wait all night, thank goodness.
Thank goodness for your sister. Were you cold?
Freezing. And the stupid thing is, we needn't have carried so much water. We had six litres each. If we'd taken less water and more warm clothes, we'd have been fine.
Six litres? That's heavy.
I know. We had to stop every twenty minutes. In hindsight, I was carrying a swimming pool on my back.
So, lessons learned?
Plenty. Next time I'll check the forecast, take a paper map, and tell someone exactly where I'm going. And I'll carry a jacket instead of a lake.
And you'll let the ranger know you're coming?
Absolutely. He wasn't angry, but he made it very clear we had been lucky.

2.title: The Circle in the Barley Field
2.topic: Past obligation, speculation and unsolved mysteries
2.focus: Modals for degrees of certainty about the past

lines.text: Welcome to Strange But True. This week, a mystery from a small farm in Wiltshire. Freya, set the scene.
So, a farmer called Tom Barker woke up last Tuesday and found a perfect circle, forty metres wide, in his barley field. Inside it, the barley was flattened in a spiral pattern.
Eerie. And it appeared overnight?
That's the baffling part. He walked the field at nine p.m. and saw nothing. At six a.m., there it was.
OK, let's not jump to conclusions. What are the explanations?
Well, first, the obvious one. It must have been made by people. Crop circles have been made by hoaxers for decades.
But in one night? In the dark?
It's possible. A group of four or five could have done it with planks and rope in about six hours. Back in the nineties, two men admitted they'd made hundreds.
Were there any clues? Footprints?
Not that the farmer saw. But it had rained, so prints might have been washed away. And there's a footpath right next to the field.
What about the wind? Could a storm have done it?
Very unlikely. Wind can't have made such a precise shape. Storms flatten crops in a messy way, not in neat spirals.
And of course, some listeners have written in saying it might have been, er, visitors from elsewhere.
Ha. I'll take that with a pinch of salt. There's no evidence for that at all.
Did anyone see anything that night?
Here's where it gets interesting. A neighbour says she saw lights in the field around two a.m. Torches, she thinks.
So the culprits may have been local students?
Possibly. Though that's purely circumstantial. Lights don't prove anything. In hindsight, the farmer wishes he'd had a camera on the field.
Has anyone come forward?
Not yet. But the circle has shed light on one thing: people love a mystery. Tom's charging three pounds to walk through it, and he's made more than he would from the barley.
Brilliant. If you know who did it, get in touch.

3.title: Walking Tour of Valparaíso
3.topic: Describing places, contrast and city vs. small-town life
3.focus: Defining & non-defining relative clauses / Order of modifiers

lines.text: Welcome, everyone, to Valparaíso, the city that's built on forty-two hills. My name's Camila, and I've lived here all my life.

We're starting at the bottom, in the old port area, which used to be one of the busiest harbours in South America. Before the Panama Canal opened, every ship that sailed between the Atlantic and the Pacific stopped here.
Sorry, so when did things change?
In 1914. Once the canal opened, the ships that had come here no longer needed to. The city went through a really difficult period.
Now, if you look up, you'll see one of our famous funiculars. This one, which was built in 1883, is still working. It takes about a minute to reach the top.
Is it safe? It looks, um, quite old.
Ha, everyone asks that. It's checked every week, I promise. The people who operate it have done it for decades.
OK, here we are at the top. These colourful old wooden houses are typical of the hill. Many of them were built by sailors, who used leftover ship paint. That's why the colours are so bright.
And look at this wall. The artist who painted this mural is a woman from the neighbourhood. Street art is everywhere here, and most of it is legal.
Legal? Really?
Yes. Owners often invite artists to paint their walls, which protects them from graffiti. A beautiful big blue whale is much harder to cover with tags.
Down this street, there's a small family-run café where you can try a local cake called a chilenito. It's two thin round biscuits with caramel inside.
And the poet's house? The one everyone talks about?
Pablo Neruda's house, which he called La Sebastiana, is a ten-minute walk from here. We'll go there after the coffee.
From his top window, you can see the whole bay, which is what he loved most about the place.
Sounds perfect. Lead the way.

3.title: Lisbon or Coimbra?
3.topic: Describing places, contrast and city vs. small-town life

lines.text: Welcome to Student Choices. Today, two students argue about where to study in Portugal. Inês studies in Lisbon, Rafael in Coimbra. Inês, why the capital?
Well, Lisbon is just so vibrant. There's always something happening. Although it's expensive, the opportunities are incredible. I've already done two internships.
Can I come in there? Lisbon's great, but it's sprawling. You spend an hour on public transport every day. In Coimbra, everything is a stone's throw from the university.
That's true, but, um, Coimbra is tiny. Once you've seen the old town, what else is there?
Actually, quite a lot. Despite its size, Coimbra is steeped in history. The university is seven hundred years old. You really soak up the atmosphere.
Rafael, isn't it a bit quiet, though?
In some ways, yes. Whereas Lisbon never sleeps, Coimbra has a more, er, human rhythm. But the student life is amazing. The traditions, the music, the capes. It's unique.
I'll admit the traditions are lovely. Nevertheless, I wanted a city where I could meet people from all over the world, not just students.
What about cost?
That's my strongest argument. My rent is half what Inês pays. Even though I earn less from part-time work, I save more.
Fair. Rents in Lisbon are crazy. On the other hand, salaries are higher, and there are more jobs.
And for weekends?
Lisbon, obviously. Beaches, concerts, new cafés springing up every week.
Coimbra's not bad, though. It's off the beaten track, so there aren't many tourists. And Porto and Lisbon are both easy to reach by train.
So, final words. Inês?
If you want energy and career opportunities, choose Lisbon, even though your wallet will suffer.
And if you want a quaint, affordable city with real student life, Coimbra is definitely worth a detour. Or, er, four years.
Thank you both.

4.title: Baking While the City Sleeps
4.topic: Sleep, daily routines and time-of-day preferences

lines.text: Most of us are fast asleep when today's guest starts work. Sean runs a bakery in Melbourne and has worked nights for eleven years. Sean, what does your day look like?
Well, my "day" starts at about ten p.m. After waking up, I have a big breakfast. Eggs, toast, the lot. People think it's strange, eating eggs at ten at night.
And then?
Then I cycle to the bakery. Arriving at about eleven, I switch on the ovens and check the doughs we prepared the afternoon before.
What's the busiest part of the night?
Between two and five. While waiting for the bread to rise, I'm shaping croissants. There's no time to sit down, honestly.
Isn't it lonely?
Not really. There are three of us. And having worked together for years, we don't need to talk much. We just, er, know what to do.
When do you finish?
About six thirty, when the first customers arrive. Before leaving, I always have one coffee with the morning staff. It's the only social part of my day.
And how do you sleep in the daytime?
That took ages to learn. Once home, I don't look at my phone. I've got blackout curtains, and I wear earplugs because of the traffic.
Do you ever feel groggy?

At first, all the time. In my first year, I was shattered. I'd power through the night and then sleep for twelve hours at weekends. Now, I'm a creature of habit. Same times, every day, even on my days off.
Even on your days off?
Yes, that's the secret. If I switch to a normal routine on Saturday, Monday night is a disaster.
Is there anything you miss?
Dinner with friends. When invited out, I usually have to say no. But I get the best bread in the city, still warm. That's worth a lot.
Sean, thank you.

lines.text: Welcome to Work Smarter. Today: giving feedback. Callum, you train managers to do this. Where do most people go wrong?

OK. Say a colleague's report is late and full of errors. It's tempting to say, "Don't worry, it's fine," and then fix it yourself. That helps nobody.

Exactly. On the other hand, it's unfair to say, "This is a disaster," in front of the whole team. It's humiliating, and it's pointless, because they'll stop listening.

And if they get defensive?
It's natural to feel defensive. It's your job to stay calm and, um, not take it personally. And it's never too late to say, "Let's talk again tomorrow."
Last tip?
It's worth remembering that feedback goes both ways. Ask your team how you're doing. It's amazing what you'll learn.

6.title: The Celebrity Who Never Came
6.topic: Rumours, journalism and unravelling a story

lines.text: My guest is Pete Hall, editor of the Bramley Gazette, a small local paper that got a big story badly wrong last spring. Pete, thanks for being so honest about it.
Well, we have to be. If we want people to trust us, we've got to admit our mistakes.
So what happened?
A reader emailed us one Friday afternoon. She said a very famous pop star had bought a house in the village. She'd seen him at the bakery that morning, apparently.
And you believed her?
Not at first. But by the evening, three more people had sent us the same rumour. One even had a blurry photo. So we thought, right, we've got to break this story before the national papers do.
Had you checked it with anyone?
That's the problem. We hadn't corroborated it properly. We'd called the estate agent, but he hadn't called back before we published. With hindsight, we should have waited.
And the story went out?
On Saturday morning. By lunchtime, there were two hundred people outside the house. Fans, photographers, a TV van.
And who actually lived there?
A retired dentist called Gerald. He'd only moved in the week before. He looks a bit like the singer, I suppose, if you've had a few drinks.
Oh no.
Yes. By the time we realised, the whole thing had been blown out of proportion. Gerald hadn't been able to leave his house for six hours.
How did you find out it was wrong?
The singer's manager called us. He was, er, not happy. The singer had been in Los Angeles all week, recording an album.
So you had to backtrack.
Completely. We published an apology on the front page, and we sent Gerald flowers. He was very kind about it, actually. He said it was the most exciting weekend he'd had in years.
What have you changed since then?
Every story now needs two independent sources. And if something sounds too good to be true, we take it with a pinch of salt. It usually is.

8.title: How Memory Champions Remember
8.topic: Psychology, memory and how the brain works

lines.text: Good morning. Today I want to talk about people known as memory champions, people competing in events where they memorise hundreds of numbers or the order of a deck of cards in under a minute.
Now, you might assume these people were born with extraordinary brains. In fact, studies carried out at several universities show that their brains look, well, pretty ordinary.
So what's the difference? Almost all of them use a technique called the method of loci, or the memory palace. It's a technique dating back to ancient Greece.
It works like this. You imagine a building you know well, your home, say.
Then you place each item to be remembered somewhere along a route through that building.
Sorry, can you give an example?

Of course. Imagine a shopping list containing eggs, bread and soap. You picture eggs smashed all over your front door, a giant loaf sitting on the sofa, soap bubbles filling the bathroom. The more vivid and ridiculous the image, the better.
Why ridiculous?
Because the brain is very good at remembering things that are strange or emotional, and very bad at remembering lists of words presented without context.

In one study, a group of volunteers with no previous training practised the method for thirty minutes a day. After six weeks, their scores had more than doubled. And retention four months later was still high.
Does it work for exams? For things like, um, dates and definitions?
It can. But there's a catch. Memorising facts isn't the same as understanding them. Students using only this method can recall a definition perfectly and still not grasp what it means.
So my advice is: use it for things that have to be learned by heart, like vocabulary or formulas. Combine it with real understanding for everything else.
Right. For homework, I'd like you to build a memory palace with ten items from today's reading list. We'll test each other on Thursday.

That's rather the point, Alex.

lines.text: Right, let's start. Last week I asked you to compare lunch habits in two countries. Sofia, you looked at Spain and the UK.

9.title: Growing Up Everywhere

lines.text: Welcome to Belonging. My guest is Adam, who's what people call a "third culture kid". Adam, what does that mean?
Basically, it means I grew up in countries that weren't my parents' country. My dad was a diplomat, so we'd move every three years. Kenya, Germany, Chile, then Thailand.
Wow. What was that like as a child?
Exciting and exhausting. I used to hate the first day at a new school. I'd stand at the door and think, "Here we go again."
How did you fit in?
I got very good at watching people. I'd figure out the norms in about a week. Who sat where, which jokes were OK, er, what you could wear. Then I'd just conform.
So you'd sort of become a different person in each place?
A bit, yes. In Germany I used to be really punctual. In Chile I became much more relaxed about time. My mum would laugh and say, "Which Adam are we getting today?"
And at home? What was your upbringing like?
Home was the one thing that stayed the same. We'd always have pancakes on Sunday, wherever we were. And my parents would speak English at home, so that was my anchor.
Did people make assumptions about you?
Constantly. People used to say, "You're American, so you must love fast food." I didn't even live in America until I was eighteen.
Ha. So stereotypes followed you around.

They did. But honestly, growing up like that made me suspicious of generalisations. When you've lived in five countries, you see that customs are deep-rooted, but people are, by and large, more similar than different.
What about now? Where do you feel at home?
That's the hardest question. I used to say "nowhere". Now I'd say "airports", which is only half a joke.
Do you want your kids to grow up the same way?
I'm not sure. I'd like them to have one place they call home. But I'd also like them to have that, um, flexibility. Maybe two countries instead of five.
Adam, thank you.

lines.text: Welcome to The Dilemma Game, where we ask each other impossible questions. Josh, you're first. Ready?

Not even fifty dollars as a reward?

Same, I think. Next one. Your best friend has a job interview, and you know he lied on his CV. The company asks you for a reference. Would you tell them?

I'd like to think so. I'd probably have second thoughts at three in the morning, though.
Ha. My turn. Ask me one.

Hmm. Honestly? It depends. If it were a small family shop, I'd go back the next day. If it were a huge supermarket, I'd, er, probably have fewer qualms about it.
Ah! So your moral compass depends on the size of the shop?
When you put it like that, it sounds terrible. But I think most people would feel the same.

11.title: The Inspector Who Spoke Up

lines.text: My guest today is Graham Pike, a former safety inspector at a food factory who reported his own company for breaking hygiene rules. Graham, thanks for coming in.
Thanks for having me. It's still not easy to talk about, so bear with me.
Take your time. What did you notice?
For about a year, I'd seen temperature records being changed. Fridges that should have been at four degrees were at nine or ten, and someone was writing "four" on the forms.
Did you say anything at the time?
Not at first. That's my biggest regret. I wish I'd spoken up straight away. I kept telling myself it wasn't my job to cause trouble.
Why did you stay quiet?
Fear, mostly. I had a mortgage, two kids. And my manager was a friend. I had real qualms about getting him into trouble. If only I'd had the courage earlier, fewer people might have got ill.
People got ill?
Yes. About forty people had food poisoning from one batch of chicken. That was when I drew the line. I couldn't look at myself in the mirror.
So you went to the authorities.
I did. I gave them copies of everything. The factory was closed for two months and fined heavily.
And what happened to you?
I lost my job, officially for "restructuring". And some colleagues stopped speaking to me. I wish they understood that I did it to protect customers, not to hurt them.
Do you ever wish you hadn't done it?
Honestly, there were nights when I had second thoughts. But no. I wish I'd done it sooner, that's all. My kids are proud of me, and that matters more than anything.
What would you say to someone in the same situation?
Write everything down, keep copies, and find someone you trust to talk to. And, um, don't wait as long as I did. Standing up for what's right gets harder the longer you leave it.
Graham, thank you for your honesty.
Thank you. I just wish this kind of thing didn't still happen.

12.title: The Accidental Expat

lines.text: In our series about people who've made a fresh start abroad, I'm talking to Ingrid, a Norwegian who's lived in Oaxaca, in Mexico, for nine years. Ingrid, you call yourself an "accidental expat". Why?
Because I never planned any of this. I came for a two-week holiday. On the last day, I missed my flight, and that changed everything.
How?
Well, I had to stay three more days, and I met a woman who ran a weaving workshop. She offered me a job. If I hadn't missed that flight, I wouldn't be living here now.
Incredible. What was the hardest part at the beginning?
The language, definitely. I only knew "hola" and "gracias". And the red tape. Getting a work visa took nearly a year. I felt like a fish out of water.
Did you ever think about going back?
Oh, often, in the first year. I was so homesick. I missed the snow, if you can believe it. If I were a less stubborn person, I'd have gone home after six months.
So being stubborn helped.
Very much. And, um, my Norwegian friends say I've changed a lot. If I hadn't moved here, I'd probably be much more serious. Mexico has made me relax.
What about the culture shock? Was it hard to acclimatise?

The heat was hard. And the pace of life. In Norway, if a meeting is at nine, it starts at nine. Here, it starts, er, when everyone arrives. If I still had my Norwegian attitude to time, I'd be stressed all day.
Have you put down roots now?
Completely. I have my own workshop with six weavers, and I'm married to a local teacher. If I'd gone home, I wouldn't have any of that.
Any advice for people thinking of moving abroad?
Learn the language before you go, if you can. I wish I had. And be patient. It broadens your horizons, but it takes time.
And do you ever miss Norway now?
I miss my family. And bread. Proper dark bread. But I go back every summer, and after two weeks, I'm ready to come home. To Oaxaca, I mean.
